content: Genital warts are a highly contagious sexually transmitted infection caused by specific subtypes of the human papillomavirus (HPV). Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during oral, genital, or anal sex with an infected partner. Genital warts are the most recognizable clinical manifestation of genital HPV infection. They are primarily caused by HPV strains 6 and 11, which are responsible for 90% of cases, though other strains such as 30, 42, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, and 54 can also be involved. Interestingly, most individuals infected with these strains do not develop warts or any other symptoms. While HPV is also a major cause of cervical cancer, with types 16 and 18 accounting for 70% of cases, the strains that cause genital warts are not associated with cancer. Although treatments can remove visible genital warts, they do not eradicate the HPV virus itself, meaning warts can recur after treatment. Historically, it was believed that the virus remained in the body for life. However, recent studies using advanced DNA detection techniques have shown that the immune system can either clear the virus or suppress it to undetectable levels. According to a 2004 report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 70% of new HPV infections clear within one year, and up to 91% clear within two years. The median duration of a new infection is approximately eight months, with the development of an effective immune response being the likely mechanism for viral clearance. The state of an individual’s immune system plays a critical role in determining their ability to clear the virus. Factors such as HIV infection, certain medications, stress, or other illnesses can impair immune function. There is also some evidence suggesting that effective treatment of visible warts may enhance the body’s immune response. Genital warts often appear in clusters and can range from being very small to forming large masses in the genital or anal regions. In women, they may occur on the external and internal surfaces of the vagina, on the cervix, or around the anus. In men, they are typically found on the tip of the penis but can also appear on the penile shaft, scrotum, or around the anus. Rarely, genital warts can develop in the mouth or throat of individuals who have engaged in oral sex with an infected partner. Genital warts may resolve spontaneously without treatment, but in some cases, they persist and develop into small, raised, flesh-colored growths. It is impossible to predict whether they will grow or disappear. Small warts can be removed through cryosurgery (freezing), electrocautery (burning), or laser treatment. Surgical removal is sometimes necessary for larger warts that do not respond to other treatments. The Gardasil vaccine, developed by Merck & Co., provides protection against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. Types 6 and 11 are responsible for genital warts, while types 16 and 18 are associated with cervical cancer. The vaccine is preventive, not therapeutic, and must be administered before exposure to the virus to be effective, ideally before the onset of sexual activity. It is widely approved for use in young women, has been tested in young men, and is approved for males in certain regions, such as the UK.
